title: Building Trust in Autonomous Systems
summary: Trust is evidence, not assertion. The five properties that produce it, why a better model produces none of them, and the numbers — pass^8 under 25%, 77% provable security — that show where the real gap sits.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**An agent is trustworthy when someone can prove it, not when someone asserts it.** A team that can name an agent's owner, show its scope, and produce its audit trail has something a regulator or a security team can inspect. A team that says "it's been tested" has an opinion.


NIST's AI Risk Management Framework puts the dependency in one line: "Trustworthy AI depends upon accountability. Accountability presupposes transparency." Not the other way around, and not optional.


Model quality is not the fix, and treating it as one is the common mistake. τ-bench measured GPT-4o at under 50% success on a single attempt at retail tasks and under 25% on all eight attempts. That gap is not a reasoning deficit you can buy your way out of. It is variance, and variance is contained by boundaries.


None of this argues the model doesn't matter. It argues that the five properties which do the work here, being bounded behavior, transparency, consistency, recoverability and a defined lifecycle, are engineering and governance decisions rather than research problems.


Start with the one that is cheapest and most load-bearing: make the scope an enforcement point rather than a document, and log the denials as well as the successes.
